claim: Destruction of oligodendrocytes and myelin sheaths in cortical gray matter profoundly alters neural activity.
source: Destruction of oligodendrocytes and myelin sheaths in cortical gray matter profoundly alters neural activity and is associated with cognitive disability in multiple sclerosis (MS).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general assertion about the effects of oligodendrocyte and myelin destruction.

claim: Destruction of oligodendrocytes and myelin sheaths in cortical gray matter is associated with cognitive disability in multiple sclerosis (MS).
source: Destruction of oligodendrocytes and myelin sheaths in cortical gray matter profoundly alters neural activity and is associated with cognitive disability in multiple sclerosis (MS).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established association between cortical demyelination and cognitive disability in MS.

claim: Myelin can be restored by regenerating oligodendrocytes from resident progenitors.
source: Myelin can be restored by regenerating oligodendrocytes from resident progenitors; however, it is not known whether regeneration restores the complex myelination patterns in cortical circuits.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about myelin regeneration.

claim: It is not known whether regeneration restores the complex myelination patterns in cortical circuits.
source: Myelin can be restored by regenerating oligodendrocytes from resident progenitors; however, it is not known whether regeneration restores the complex myelination patterns in cortical circuits.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: The pattern of myelination in cortex changed dramatically after regeneration.
source: These longitudinal studies revealed that the pattern of myelination in cortex changed dramatically after regeneration, as new oligodendrocytes were formed in different locations and new sheaths were often established along axon segments previously lacking myelin.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by longitudinal in vivo imaging data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: New oligodendrocytes were formed in different locations after regeneration.
source: These longitudinal studies revealed that the pattern of myelination in cortex changed dramatically after regeneration, as new oligodendrocytes were formed in different locations and new sheaths were often established along axon segments previously lacking myelin.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by spatial analysis of oligodendrocyte positions shown in Figure 3.

claim: New sheaths were often established along axon segments previously lacking myelin after regeneration.
source: These longitudinal studies revealed that the pattern of myelination in cortex changed dramatically after regeneration, as new oligodendrocytes were formed in different locations and new sheaths were often established along axon segments previously lacking myelin.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by myelin sheath tracing data presented in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Oligodendrogenesis was persistently impaired in deeper cortical layers that experienced higher gliosis.
source: Despite the dramatic increase in axonal territory available, oligodendrogenesis was persistently impaired in deeper cortical layers that experienced higher gliosis.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by layer-specific analysis in Figure 2 and gliosis data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Repeated reorganization of myelin patterns in MS may alter circuit function and contribute to cognitive decline.
source: Repeated reorganization of myelin patterns in MS may alter circuit function and contribute to cognitive decline.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion stated in the abstract based on the findings of altered myelination patterns.

claim: Oligodendrocytes form concentric sheets of membrane around axons that enhance the speed of action potential propagation.
source: Oligodendrocytes form concentric sheets of membrane around axons that enhance the speed of action potential propagation, provide metabolic support and control neuronal excitability through ion homeostasis.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about oligodendrocyte function.

claim: Oligodendrocytes provide metabolic support to axons.
source: Oligodendrocytes form concentric sheets of membrane around axons that enhance the speed of action potential propagation, provide metabolic support and control neuronal excitability through ion homeostasis.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about oligodendrocyte function.

claim: Oligodendrocytes control neuronal excitability through ion homeostasis.
source: Oligodendrocytes form concentric sheets of membrane around axons that enhance the speed of action potential propagation, provide metabolic support and control neuronal excitability through ion homeostasis.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about oligodendrocyte function.

claim: Loss of oligodendrocytes and myelin can alter the firing behavior of neurons.
source: Consequently, loss of oligodendrocytes and myelin can alter the firing behavior of neurons and impair their survival, leading to profound disability in diseases such as multiple sclerosis (MS), in which the immune system inappropriately targets myelin for destruction.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about the consequences of oligodendrocyte loss.

claim: Loss of oligodendrocytes and myelin can impair neuronal survival.
source: Consequently, loss of oligodendrocytes and myelin can alter the firing behavior of neurons and impair their survival, leading to profound disability in diseases such as multiple sclerosis (MS), in which the immune system inappropriately targets myelin for destruction.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about the consequences of oligodendrocyte loss.

claim: In multiple sclerosis, the immune system inappropriately targets myelin for destruction.
source: Consequently, loss of oligodendrocytes and myelin can alter the firing behavior of neurons and impair their survival, leading to profound disability in diseases such as multiple sclerosis (MS), in which the immune system inappropriately targets myelin for destruction.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about MS pathology.

claim: The CNS is capable of spontaneous remyelination through mobilization of oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) in both relapsing-remitting forms of MS and the cuprizone model of demyelination in mouse.
source: In both relapsing-remitting forms of MS and the cuprizone model of demyelination in mouse, the CNS is capable of spontaneous remyelination through mobilization of oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) (Baxi et al., 2017; Chang et al., 2000; Chang et al., 2012), which remain abundant in both gray and white matter throughout adulthood (Dimou et al., 2008; Hughes et al., 2013; Young et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations to previous studies.

claim: OPCs remain abundant in both gray and white matter throughout adulthood.
source: In both relapsing-remitting forms of MS and the cuprizone model of demyelination in mouse, the CNS is capable of spontaneous remyelination through mobilization of oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) (Baxi et al., 2017; Chang et al., 2000; Chang et al., 2012), which remain abundant in both gray and white matter throughout adulthood (Dimou et al., 2008; Hughes et al., 2013; Young et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations to previous studies.

claim: Demyelination is prevalent in cortical gray matter of MS patients.
source: In vivo studies of remyelination have focused primarily on white matter, where assessments of myelin are aided by the high density and symmetrical alignment of myelin sheaths; however, postmortem histological analysis (Kidd et al., 1999; Kutzelnigg et al., 2005; Lucchinetti et al., 2011; Peterson et al., 2001) and new in vivo MRI and PET imaging methods (Beck et al., 2018; Filippi et al., 2014; Herranz et al., 2019; Kilsdonk et al., 2013; Magliozzi et al., 2018) indicate that demyelination is also prevalent in cortical gray matter of MS patients.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations to postmortem and imaging studies.

claim: Cortical lesion load correlates with signs of physical and cognitive disability in MS patients.
source: Cortical lesion load correlates with signs of physical and cognitive disability, including cognitive impairment, fatigue and memory loss (Calabrese et al., 2012; Nielsen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Myelination patterns in the cerebral cortex are highly variable, with sheath content varying between cortical regions, among different types of neurons and even along the length of individual axons.
source: Unlike white matter, myelination patterns in the cerebral cortex are highly variable, with sheath content varying between cortical regions, among different types of neurons and even along the length of individual axons (Micheva et al., 2016; Tomassy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Both oligodendrocytes and individual myelin sheaths are remarkably stable in the adult brain.
source: Despite this evidence of discontinuous myelination, recent in vivo imaging studies indicate that both oligodendrocytes and individual myelin sheaths are remarkably stable in the adult brain (Hill et al., 2018; Hughes et al., 2018), suggesting that maintaining precise sheath placement is important for cortical function.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations to recent imaging studies.

claim: Maintaining precise sheath placement is important for cortical function.
source: Despite this evidence of discontinuous myelination, recent in vivo imaging studies indicate that both oligodendrocytes and individual myelin sheaths are remarkably stable in the adult brain (Hill et al., 2018; Hughes et al., 2018), suggesting that maintaining precise sheath placement is important for cortical function.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an inference from the stability of myelin sheaths.

claim: More than 90% of the baseline population of oligodendrocytes within the upper layers of cortex degenerated after three weeks of cuprizone treatment.
source: When mice were fed cuprizone for three weeks,>90% of the baseline population of oligodendrocytes within the upper layers of cortex degenerated (94.2 ± 0.05%; N = 6 mice, mean ± SEM) (Figure 1E,G,I; Video 3), with most cell loss occurring after cessation of cuprizone exposure (Figure 1I,J).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by longitudinal imaging data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Most oligodendrocyte cell loss occurred after cessation of cuprizone exposure.
source: When mice were fed cuprizone for three weeks,>90% of the baseline population of oligodendrocytes within the upper layers of cortex degenerated (94.2 ± 0.05%; N = 6 mice, mean ± SEM) (Figure 1E,G,I; Video 3), with most cell loss occurring after cessation of cuprizone exposure (Figure 1I,J).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by temporal analysis shown in Figure 1I,J.

claim: Only about half of the oligodendrocytes (55.2 ± 0.03%) were replaced after nine weeks of recovery.
source: New oligodendrocytes initially appeared rapidly during the recovery phase (Figure 1K); however, this burst of oligodendrogenesis was not sustained, and as a consequence, only about half of the oligodendrocytes (55.2 ± 0.03%) were replaced after nine weeks of recovery.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by longitudinal cell tracking data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Oligodendrocyte regeneration is much slower and less complete in cortical gray matter than in white matter.
source: These results indicate that although a prominent regenerative response is initiated in cortical gray matter, oligodendrocyte regeneration is much slower (Baxi et al., 2017) and less complete than in white matter (Baxi et al., 2017; Gudi et al., 2009; Jeffery and Blakemore, 1995; Matsushima and Morell, 2001).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study, comparing the current findings to previous studies in white matter cited in the text.

claim: Cuprizone-treated animals did not experience extensive axonal loss.
source: These sections exhibited comparable neurofilament-L immunoreactivity, suggesting that cuprizone-treated animals did not experience extensive axonal loss and therefore is unlikely to be responsible for impaired oligodendrocyte regeneration in the cortex.
evidence: This is a finding from post-hoc immunostaining analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Oligodendrocyte recovery was highly efficient in the top 100 μm zone, reaching 85.2 ± 0.17% of the baseline oligodendrocyte population nine weeks after cuprizone.
source: Oligodendrocyte recovery was highly efficient in the top 100 μm zone, reaching 85.2 ± 0.17% of the baseline oligodendrocyte population nine weeks after cuprizone, but only 55.5 ± 0.11% of baseline after 9 weeks in the bottom 100 μm zone (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from layer-specific analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Oligodendrocyte recovery in the bottom 100 μm zone reached only 55.5 ± 0.11% of baseline after 9 weeks.
source: Oligodendrocyte recovery was highly efficient in the top 100 μm zone, reaching 85.2 ± 0.17% of the baseline oligodendrocyte population nine weeks after cuprizone, but only 55.5 ± 0.11% of baseline after 9 weeks in the bottom 100 μm zone (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from layer-specific analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There was a proportionally higher rate of cell loss in the bottom 100 μm zone compared to the upper zone during the first 2 weeks of recovery post-cuprizone.
source: During this period, there was both a proportionally higher rate of cell loss and lower rate of cell replacement in the bottom 100 μm zone compared to the upper zone (Figure 2F,G) (loss @ week 4, p=0.044; addition @ week 4, p=0.036, N-way ANOVA with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons), indicating that the ability to balance cell loss with replacement declines with depth during this initial period.
evidence: This is a primary finding from layer-specific temporal analysis shown in Figure 2F,G with statistical testing.

claim: There was a lower rate of cell replacement in the bottom 100 μm zone compared to the upper zone during the first 2 weeks of recovery post-cuprizone.
source: During this period, there was both a proportionally higher rate of cell loss and lower rate of cell replacement in the bottom 100 μm zone compared to the upper zone (Figure 2F,G) (loss @ week 4, p=0.044; addition @ week 4, p=0.036, N-way ANOVA with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons), indicating that the ability to balance cell loss with replacement declines with depth during this initial period.
evidence: This is a primary finding from layer-specific temporal analysis shown in Figure 2F,G with statistical testing.

claim: The ability to balance cell loss with replacement declines with depth during the initial recovery period.
source: During this period, there was both a proportionally higher rate of cell loss and lower rate of cell replacement in the bottom 100 μm zone compared to the upper zone (Figure 2F,G) (loss @ week 4, p=0.044; addition @ week 4, p=0.036, N-way ANOVA with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons), indicating that the ability to balance cell loss with replacement declines with depth during this initial period.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the layer-specific data shown in Figure 2F,G.

claim: There was no evidence of persistent OPC depletion during recovery.
source: Although OPCs are slightly less abundant in the deeper layers compared to the surface 100 μm (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,C,D) (p=2.084×10–13, N-way ANOVA, by depth), there was no evidence of persistent OPC depletion during recovery (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,F) (p=0.086, Kruskal-Wallis one-way ANOVA).
evidence: This is a finding from immunostaining analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 with statistical testing.

claim: GFAP+ astrocytes increased nearly 10-fold in the deeper (200–500 μm) regions of cortex following cuprizone-treatment.
source: GFAP+ astrocytes are relatively rare in the deeper (200–500 μm) regions of cortex in naive mice; however, following cuprizone-treatment, their number increased nearly 10-fold (p=5.86×10−16, N-way ANOVA, by time-point).
evidence: This is a finding from immunostaining analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 with statistical testing.

claim: Enhanced GFAP expression in deeper cortical layers remained elevated throughout the recovery period.
source: This enhanced GFAP expression remained elevated throughout the recovery period (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G) (p=0.006, Kruskal-Wallis one-way ANOVA, with Fisher's correction for multiple comparisons) and they retained a reactive morphology, even after 5 weeks of recovery (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B,E,G).
evidence: This is a finding from immunostaining analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 with statistical testing.

claim: Regenerated oligodendrocytes occupied positions within the parenchyma that are distinct from those present at baseline.
source: These results demonstrate that regenerated oligodendrocytes occupy locations within the parenchyma that are distinct from those present at baseline, and therefore may establish a new pattern of myelination.
evidence: This is a conclusion from spatial analysis of oligodendrocyte positions shown in Figure 3.

claim: Regenerated oligodendrocytes were significantly displaced relative to oligodendrocyte positions prior to degeneration.
source: In contrast, regenerated oligodendrocytes added to the cortex of cuprizone-treated mice were significantly displaced relative to oligodendrocyte positions prior to degeneration (Figure 3C, All Cells vs. Self-self) (p=8.95×10−7, N-way ANOVA with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons).
evidence: This is a primary finding from spatial analysis shown in Figure 3C with statistical testing.

claim: Regenerated oligodendrocytes produced similar numbers of sheaths as control cells (Control: 53 ± 3 sheaths; Regenerated: 51 ± 2 sheaths).
source: Although regenerated oligodendrocytes had access to much more axonal territory, they produced similar numbers of sheaths (Figure 3E) (Control: 53 ± 3 sheaths, 10 cells, N = 3 mice; Regenerated: 51 ± 2 sheaths, 9 cells, N = 3 mice, p=0.628, unpaired two-tailed t-test).
evidence: This is a primary finding from morphological reconstruction analysis shown in Figure 3E with statistical testing.

claim: Regenerated cells formed more total myelin than control cells (Control: 3.17 ± 0.16 mm; Regenerated: 3.80 ± 0.23 mm).
source: However, regenerated cells formed more total myelin (Figure 3F) (Total sheath length: Control, 3.17 ± 0.16 mm; Regenerated: 3.80 ± 0.23 mm, p=0.041, unpaired two-tailed t-test) by extending slightly longer sheaths (Figure 3G) (average sheath length: Control, 62.6 ± 2.6 μm; Regenerated, 72.3 ± 2.2 μm, p=0.012, unpaired two-tailed t-test), despite having similar distributions of sheath lengths (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is a primary finding from morphological reconstruction analysis shown in Figure 3F with statistical testing.

claim: Regenerated cells extended slightly longer sheaths than control cells (Control: 62.6 ± 2.6 μm; Regenerated: 72.3 ± 2.2 μm).
source: However, regenerated cells formed more total myelin (Figure 3F) (Total sheath length: Control, 3.17 ± 0.16 mm; Regenerated: 3.80 ± 0.23 mm, p=0.041, unpaired two-tailed t-test) by extending slightly longer sheaths (Figure 3G) (average sheath length: Control, 62.6 ± 2.6 μm; Regenerated, 72.3 ± 2.2 μm, p=0.012, unpaired two-tailed t-test), despite having similar distributions of sheath lengths (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is a primary finding from morphological reconstruction analysis shown in Figure 3G with statistical testing.

claim: Regenerated oligodendrocytes have morphologies remarkably similar to cells added to existing myelinated networks in naïve mice.
source: Thus, regenerated oligodendrocytes formed in an environment with greater myelination targets have morphologies remarkably similar to cells added to existing myelinated networks in naïve mice, suggesting that oligodendrocyte structure is shaped by strong cell intrinsic mechanisms.
evidence: This is a conclusion from morphological analysis shown in Figure 3, comparing control and regenerated cells.

claim: Oligodendrocyte structure is shaped by strong cell intrinsic mechanisms.
source: Thus, regenerated oligodendrocytes formed in an environment with greater myelination targets have morphologies remarkably similar to cells added to existing myelinated networks in naïve mice, suggesting that oligodendrocyte structure is shaped by strong cell intrinsic mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the similarity in morphology between control and regenerated oligodendrocytes despite different environments.

claim: Regenerated oligodendrocytes in cuprizone exposed mice exhibit only 59.1 ± 5.8% territory overlap with oligodendrocytes that originally populated these regions of the cortex.
source: This analysis revealed that regenerated oligodendrocytes in cuprizone exposed mice exhibit only 59.1 ± 5.8% territory overlap (Range: 37.2–79.0%, N = 6) with oligodendrocytes that originally populated these regions of the cortex.
evidence: This is a primary finding from territory overlap analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Regenerated cell territories enclosed an average volume of 116 ± 14.1% of the total territory at baseline.
source: Moreover, because regenerated cell territories were larger (Figure 4B), they enclosed an average volume of 116 ± 14.1% of the total territory at baseline (Range: 87.4–181%) (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a primary finding from territory analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: 84.4 ± 2.7% of myelin sheaths were destroyed in the top 100 μm zone after cuprizone treatment.
source: In mice treated with cuprizone, 84.4 ± 2.7% of myelin sheaths were destroyed in this region (Figure 5B), but sheath numbers were restored to baseline levels after five weeks (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from myelin sheath tracing analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Sheath numbers were restored to baseline levels after five weeks of recovery.
source: In mice treated with cuprizone, 84.4 ± 2.7% of myelin sheaths were destroyed in this region (Figure 5B), but sheath numbers were restored to baseline levels after five weeks (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from myelin sheath tracing analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Only 50.5 ± 2.9% of specific internodes were replaced after recovery.
source: However, despite this apparent recovery of overall myelin content, only 50.5 ± 2.9% of specific internodes were replaced, 32.4 ± 1.2% were lost (not replaced) and 47.6 ± 9.9% novel internodes were formed (N = 5 mice) (Figure 5D), indicating that regeneration leads to a dramatic change in the overall pattern of myelin within cortical circuits.
evidence: This is a primary finding from myelin sheath fate analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: 32.4 ± 1.2% of internodes were lost (not replaced) after recovery.
source: However, despite this apparent recovery of overall myelin content, only 50.5 ± 2.9% of specific internodes were replaced, 32.4 ± 1.2% were lost (not replaced) and 47.6 ± 9.9% novel internodes were formed (N = 5 mice) (Figure 5D), indicating that regeneration leads to a dramatic change in the overall pattern of myelin within cortical circuits.
evidence: This is a primary finding from myelin sheath fate analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: 47.6 ± 9.9% novel internodes were formed after recovery.
source: However, despite this apparent recovery of overall myelin content, only 50.5 ± 2.9% of specific internodes were replaced, 32.4 ± 1.2% were lost (not replaced) and 47.6 ± 9.9% novel internodes were formed (N = 5 mice) (Figure 5D), indicating that regeneration leads to a dramatic change in the overall pattern of myelin within cortical circuits.
evidence: This is a primary finding from myelin sheath fate analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Regeneration leads to a dramatic change in the overall pattern of myelin within cortical circuits.
source: However, despite this apparent recovery of overall myelin content, only 50.5 ± 2.9% of specific internodes were replaced, 32.4 ± 1.2% were lost (not replaced) and 47.6 ± 9.9% novel internodes were formed (N = 5 mice) (Figure 5D), indicating that regeneration leads to a dramatic change in the overall pattern of myelin within cortical circuits.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the myelin sheath fate analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Oligodendrocytes regenerated in regions that originally had a high density of sheaths devoted a larger proportion of their sheaths to replacement.
source: Analysis of single oligodendrocytes revealed that the degree of sheath replacement varied considerably between regions. Oligodendrocytes regenerated in regions that originally had a high density of sheaths devoted a larger proportion of their sheaths to replacement (R2 = 0.4232, 13 cells, N = 4 mice) (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is a primary finding from single cell analysis shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: The majority of replaced internodes had at least one neighbor (79.5 ± 2.5%).
source: While lost (not replaced) and novel internodes exhibited an equal proportion of isolated and neighbored sheaths, the majority of replaced internodes had at least one neighbor (79.5 ± 2.5%) (Figure 6H), visible in the bias toward higher values in the lower right quadrant in the myelination matrix (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is a primary finding from myelin pattern analysis shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Regenerated oligodendrocytes preferentially formed sheaths on axons that were previously more heavily myelinated.
source: These data suggest that regenerated oligodendrocytes preferentially formed sheaths on axons that were previously more heavily myelinated, suggesting that factors which promote greater myelination of specific axons are preserved after demyelination.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the myelin pattern analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Factors which promote greater myelination of specific axons are preserved after demyelination.
source: These data suggest that regenerated oligodendrocytes preferentially formed sheaths on axons that were previously more heavily myelinated, suggesting that factors which promote greater myelination of specific axons are preserved after demyelination.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that replaced sheaths preferentially had neighbors.

claim: Myelin sheaths were often reformed at a similar position along axons.
source: Remarkably, myelin sheaths were often reformed at a similar position along axons, even when sheaths were isolated from neighboring sheaths and therefore could have extended over a much larger area.
evidence: This is a primary finding from longitudinal imaging analysis shown in Figure 7A and Video 10.

claim: In Mobp-EGFP mice, complete oligodendrocyte morphologies could be resolved in vivo, including cytoplasmic processes and individual myelin internodes within the upper layers of the cortex.
source: In these mice, complete oligodendrocyte morphologies could be resolved in vivo, including cytoplasmic processes and individual myelin internodes within the upper layers of the cortex.
evidence: This describes the capabilities of the Mobp-EGFP mouse model used in the study.

claim: Oligodendrocytes in the cortex ensheath a select group of axons, including long-range axonal projections oriented horizontally to the pia.
source: In these regions, oligodendrocytes ensheath a select group of axons, including long-range axonal projections oriented horizontally to the pia (Bock et al., 2011; Figure 1B), and in deeper layers, vertically-oriented axons belonging to both local cortical neurons and long-range projections (Figure 1A,C).
evidence: This describes the myelination pattern in cortex, supported by citation and imaging data in Figure 1.

claim: Cuprizone is a copper chelator that induces robust fragmentation and apoptosis of oligodendrocytes.
source: To induce demyelination, young adult Mobp-EGFP mice (age 8–12 weeks) were fed chow mixed with 0.2% cuprizone, a copper chelator that induces robust fragmentation and apoptosis of oligodendrocytes (Vega-Riquer et al., 2019; Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and multiple volumes (425 μm x 425 μm x 550 μm) corresponding to layers I–IV were imaged repeatedly prior to injury, during demyelination and through recovery for up to 12 weeks (Figure 1D; Video 1).
evidence: This describes the mechanism of cuprizone, supported by citation and imaging data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Oligodendrocytes and individual myelin sheaths are extraordinarily stable in the adult brain.
source: Oligodendrocytes and individual myelin sheaths are extraordinarily stable in the adult brain (Hill et al., 2018; Hughes et al., 2018; Yeung et al., 2014); however, the amount of myelin within these circuits is not static, as new oligodendrocytes continue to be generated in the adult CNS, each of which produces dozens of sheaths (Hughes et al., 2018; Kang et al., 2010; Xiao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: New oligodendrocytes continue to be generated in the adult CNS, each of which produces dozens of sheaths.
source: Oligodendrocytes and individual myelin sheaths are extraordinarily stable in the adult brain (Hill et al., 2018; Hughes et al., 2018; Yeung et al., 2014); however, the amount of myelin within these circuits is not static, as new oligodendrocytes continue to be generated in the adult CNS, each of which produces dozens of sheaths (Hughes et al., 2018; Kang et al., 2010; Xiao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Oligodendrogenesis declines with age in both control and cuprizone-treated mice.
source: However, as oligodendrogenesis declines with age in both control and cuprizone-treated mice (Figure 1K), cuprizone-treated mice may never reach a normal oligodendrocyte density after demyelination.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, supported by data in Figure 1K.

claim: Cuprizone-treated mice may never reach a normal oligodendrocyte density after demyelination.
source: However, as oligodendrogenesis declines with age in both control and cuprizone-treated mice (Figure 1K), cuprizone-treated mice may never reach a normal oligodendrocyte density after demyelination.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the observed decline in oligodendrogenesis with age.

claim: Axonal degeneration has been observed in the experimental allergic encephalomyelitis (EAE) demyelinating model.
source: Axonal degeneration has been observed in the experimental allergic encephalomyelitis (EAE) demyelinating model (Mei et al., 2016), and there is evidence of cortical axon pathology in the corpus callosum after prolonged exposure to cuprizone (Gudi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: There is evidence of cortical axon pathology in the corpus callosum after prolonged exposure to cuprizone.
source: Axonal degeneration has been observed in the experimental allergic encephalomyelitis (EAE) demyelinating model (Mei et al., 2016), and there is evidence of cortical axon pathology in the corpus callosum after prolonged exposure to cuprizone (Gudi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citation.

claim: The proportional rates of oligodendrocyte addition were similar between the top zone (0–100 μm) and bottom zone (200–300 μm) in control mice.
source: In control mice, the proportional rates of oligodendrocyte addition were similar between the top zone (0–100 μm) and bottom zone (200–300 μm) (top: 2.62 ± 0.37%; bottom: 2.93 ± 0.26% per week), despite their dramatically different oligodendrocyte densities (0–100 μm: 17 ± 2 cells; 200–300 μm: 79 ± 10 cells, N = 11 mice @ baseline) (Figure 2D,E); the only exception was for time points when no cells were incorporated into the top zone (Figure 2E, p=0.0036 @ 5 weeks, N-way ANOVA with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons).
evidence: This is a finding from layer-specific analysis in control mice shown in Figure 2D,E with statistical testing.

claim: Oligodendrocyte enrichment in deeper layers occurs early in development, but then proceeds at similar proportional rates across cortical layers in adulthood.
source: These findings suggest that oligodendrocyte enrichment in deeper layers occurs early in development, but then proceeds at similar proportional rates across cortical layers in adulthood.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of similar proportional rates of oligodendrocyte addition across layers in adult mice.

claim: The larger number of oligodendrocytes that degenerate in deeper layers may inhibit regeneration by creating more inflammation and myelin debris.
source: The larger number of oligodendrocytes that degenerate in this area may inhibit regeneration by creating more inflammation and myelin debris, factors known to suppress oligodendrogenesis.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed impaired regeneration in deeper layers.

claim: Inflammation and myelin debris are factors known to suppress oligodendrogenesis.
source: The larger number of oligodendrocytes that degenerate in this area may inhibit regeneration by creating more inflammation and myelin debris, factors known to suppress oligodendrogenesis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Reactive gliosis was more prominent and more prolonged in deeper layers of cortex.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, reactive gliosis was more prominent and more prolonged in deeper layers of cortex (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B,E,G).
evidence: This is a finding from immunostaining analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: GLI1-expressing glial progenitors positioned within germinal zones along the lateral ventricles are mobilized in response to cuprizone-induced demyelination.
source: Although recent studies indicate that GLI1-expressing glial progenitors positioned within germinal zones along the lateral ventricles are mobilized in response to cuprizone-induced demyelination, forming new OPCs that migrate and differentiate into oligodendrocytes with higher probability than resident OPCs (Samanta et al., 2015), our results indicate that this recruitment is not sufficient in the short term to overcome existing inhibitory barriers within cortical gray matter.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citation.

claim: GLI1-expressing glial progenitors form new OPCs that migrate and differentiate into oligodendrocytes with higher probability than resident OPCs.
source: Although recent studies indicate that GLI1-expressing glial progenitors positioned within germinal zones along the lateral ventricles are mobilized in response to cuprizone-induced demyelination, forming new OPCs that migrate and differentiate into oligodendrocytes with higher probability than resident OPCs (Samanta et al., 2015), our results indicate that this recruitment is not sufficient in the short term to overcome existing inhibitory barriers within cortical gray matter.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citation.

claim: Recruitment of GLI1-expressing glial progenitors is not sufficient in the short term to overcome existing inhibitory barriers within cortical gray matter.
source: Although recent studies indicate that GLI1-expressing glial progenitors positioned within germinal zones along the lateral ventricles are mobilized in response to cuprizone-induced demyelination, forming new OPCs that migrate and differentiate into oligodendrocytes with higher probability than resident OPCs (Samanta et al., 2015), our results indicate that this recruitment is not sufficient in the short term to overcome existing inhibitory barriers within cortical gray matter.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observed incomplete recovery despite GLI1+ progenitor mobilization.

claim: OPCs exhibit a decline in regenerative potential with age and can undergo senescence.
source: Like other progenitor cells, OPCs exhibit a decline in regenerative potential with age and can undergo senescence, a process that may be accelerated by exposure to inflammatory cytokines (Kirby et al., 2019; Neumann et al., 2019; Nicaise et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: OPC senescence may be accelerated by exposure to inflammatory cytokines.
source: Like other progenitor cells, OPCs exhibit a decline in regenerative potential with age and can undergo senescence, a process that may be accelerated by exposure to inflammatory cytokines (Kirby et al., 2019; Neumann et al., 2019; Nicaise et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Certain aspects of the inflammatory response strongly promote OPC differentiation.
source: In this regard, evidence that certain aspects of the inflammatory response strongly promote OPC differentiation (Kotter et al., 2006; Miron et al., 2013; Ruckh et al., 2012) raises the possibility that there is a critical time window for optimal repair.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: There may be a critical time window for optimal repair after demyelination.
source: In this regard, evidence that certain aspects of the inflammatory response strongly promote OPC differentiation (Kotter et al., 2006; Miron et al., 2013; Ruckh et al., 2012) raises the possibility that there is a critical time window for optimal repair.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the role of inflammation in promoting OPC differentiation.

claim: Regenerated oligodendrocytes underwent a similar period of structural refinement over a period of ~10 days.
source: Complete reconstruction of individual oligodendrocytes revealed that regenerated cells underwent a similar period of structural refinement over a period of ~10 days and ultimately formed a comparable number of sheaths (Figure 3D,E; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–J).
evidence: This is a finding from longitudinal reconstruction analysis shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The initial dynamics of newly formed oligodendrocytes are remarkably similar to those described in the developing zebrafish spinal cord.
source: Notably, the initial dynamics of these newly formed oligodendrocytes are remarkably similar to those described in the developing zebrafish spinal cord (Auer et al., 2018; Czopka et al., 2013), suggesting that the maturation sequence of oligodendrocytes is both highly conserved and cell intrinsic.
evidence: This is a comparison to previous studies with supporting citations.

claim: The maturation sequence of oligodendrocytes is both highly conserved and cell intrinsic.
source: Notably, the initial dynamics of these newly formed oligodendrocytes are remarkably similar to those described in the developing zebrafish spinal cord (Auer et al., 2018; Czopka et al., 2013), suggesting that the maturation sequence of oligodendrocytes is both highly conserved and cell intrinsic.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the similarity in oligodendrocyte dynamics across species.

claim: The morphological plasticity of newly formed oligodendrocytes lasts for more than 1 week in the cortex.
source: This time-lapse analysis revealed that the morphological plasticity of newly formed oligodendrocytes lasts for more than 1 week in the cortex (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I,J); therefore, comparisons between control and regenerated oligodendrocytes were made from cells 12–14 days after first appearance when they reached their mature form.
evidence: This is a finding from time-lapse analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1I,J.

claim: The size and shape of oligodendrocytes is profoundly limited by cell intrinsic mechanisms.
source: As regenerated oligodendrocytes are formed in an environment with an apparent surplus of receptive axons, these findings suggest that the size and shape of oligodendrocytes is profoundly limited by cell intrinsic mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that regenerated oligodendrocytes have similar morphologies despite more available axonal territory.

claim: Shadow plaques are classically considered to represent partially remyelinated axons.
source: This hypothesis is based on evidence that 'shadow plaques', which are classically considered to represent partially remyelinated axons (Lassmann et al., 1997), did not appear to contain many newly born oligodendrocytes, as assessed using C14–based birth dating; the progressive decline in atmospheric C14 levels following the cessation of atomic testing in the 1950s allow the date of last cell division to be estimated the amount of C14 present.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citation.

claim: Oligodendrocytes can be generated through direct differentiation of OPCs without cell division in the adult mouse brain.
source: Although in vivo imaging studies in the adult mouse brain indicate that oligodendrocytes can be generated through direct differentiation of OPCs without cell division (Hughes et al., 2013), potentially confounding measures of cell age based on proliferation, these results nevertheless posit that significant new myelin may be created by existing oligodendrocytes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citation.

claim: The few oligodendrocytes that survived cuprizone did not contribute substantial new myelin.
source: In our studies, the few oligodendrocytes that survived cuprizone did not contribute substantial new myelin.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on longitudinal imaging observations.

claim: The cuprizone model does not fully recapitulate the pathology of cortical lesions observed in MS.
source: However, the cuprizone model does not fully recapitulate the pathology of cortical lesions observed in MS.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the cuprizone model.

claim: Demyelination of the upper layers of the cortex in autopsy samples from MS patients are correlated with regions of leptomeningeal inflammation.
source: In particular, demyelination of the upper layers of the cortex in autopsy samples from MS patients are correlated with regions of leptomeningeal inflammation, composed of B and T cells that secrete cytotoxic cytokines and create a complex inflammatory milieu (Howell et al., 2011; Magliozzi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: When a regenerated oligodendrocyte had access to a territory that was previously myelinated, it was capable of establishing sheaths along axons that were previously myelinated.
source: However, when a regenerated oligodendrocyte had access to a territory that was previously myelinated, it was capable of establishing sheaths along axons that were previously myelinated, indicating that the local factors which initially influenced axon selection were retained after demyelination.
evidence: This is a finding from single cell analysis of myelin sheath replacement.

claim: The local factors which initially influenced axon selection were retained after demyelination.
source: However, when a regenerated oligodendrocyte had access to a territory that was previously myelinated, it was capable of establishing sheaths along axons that were previously myelinated, indicating that the local factors which initially influenced axon selection were retained after demyelination.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that regenerated oligodendrocytes can remyelinate previously myelinated axons.

claim: It is extremely rare for neighboring cortical axons to share a similar trajectory over ~60–70 µm.
source: As a result, it is extremely rare for neighboring cortical axons to share a similar trajectory over ~60–70 µm, the typical length of a myelin sheath, increasing the likelihood that similarly positioned sheaths represent remeylination of the same axon.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of cortical axon trajectories that supports the inference of specific axon remyelination.

claim: Previous studies suggest that components of the NOR are redistributed after demyelination in the PNS.
source: Although previous studies suggest that components of the NOR are redistributed after demyelination in the PNS (England et al., 1990) and in MS lesions (Coman et al., 2006; Craner et al., 2004; Dupree et al., 2004), our studies reveal that βIV-spectrin, which forms a complex with Ankyrin-G to link voltage-gated sodium channels to the actin cytoskeleton at NORs (Susuki et al., 2016), remains clustered (without flanking myelin sheaths) with continued administration of cuprizone for up to six weeks (Figure 7D,F), suggesting that nodal guideposts remain for many weeks after demyelination.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Previous studies suggest that components of the NOR are redistributed after demyelination in MS lesions.
source: Although previous studies suggest that components of the NOR are redistributed after demyelination in the PNS (England et al., 1990) and in MS lesions (Coman et al., 2006; Craner et al., 2004; Dupree et al., 2004), our studies reveal that βIV-spectrin, which forms a complex with Ankyrin-G to link voltage-gated sodium channels to the actin cytoskeleton at NORs (Susuki et al., 2016), remains clustered (without flanking myelin sheaths) with continued administration of cuprizone for up to six weeks (Figure 7D,F), suggesting that nodal guideposts remain for many weeks after demyelination.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: βIV-spectrin forms a complex with Ankyrin-G to link voltage-gated sodium channels to the actin cytoskeleton at NORs.
source: Although previous studies suggest that components of the NOR are redistributed after demyelination in the PNS (England et al., 1990) and in MS lesions (Coman et al., 2006; Craner et al., 2004; Dupree et al., 2004), our studies reveal that βIV-spectrin, which forms a complex with Ankyrin-G to link voltage-gated sodium channels to the actin cytoskeleton at NORs (Susuki et al., 2016), remains clustered (without flanking myelin sheaths) with continued administration of cuprizone for up to six weeks (Figure 7D,F), suggesting that nodal guideposts remain for many weeks after demyelination.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citation.

claim: Stabilizing the structural elements of previously myelinated axonal domains could represent a potential target for remyelinating therapies.
source: Stabilizing the structural elements of previously myelinated axonal domains could therefore represent a potential target for remyelinating therapies.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion based on the finding that nodal components persist after demyelination.

claim: Differences in axonal diameter do not influence remyelination following oligodendrocyte ablation.
source: More widespread structural reorganization of demyelinated axons, resulting in changes to axonal diameter, might also alter the distribution of replaced myelin sheaths, although a recent pre-print suggests that differences in axonal diameter do not influence remyelination following oligodendrocyte ablation (Snaidero et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from a recent pre-print with supporting citation.

claim: The reorganization of myelin that occurs in cortical circuits during regeneration may have profound functional consequences on cognition and behavior.
source: Thus, the reorganization of myelin that occurs in cortical circuits during regeneration may have profound functional consequences on cognition and behavior.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion about the potential functional implications of the findings.

claim: Demyelination triggers a dramatic decrease in excitatory synapses.
source: Moreover, many neurodegenerative diseases and affective disorders are associated with profound alterations in myelin (Gouw et al., 2008; Ihara et al., 2010; Stedehouder and Kushner, 2017), and recent studies indicate that demyelination triggers a dramatic decrease in excitatory synapses (Araújo et al., 2017; Werneburg et al., 2020), suggesting that disruptions in these sheaths may also influence both structural and functional aspects of circuits.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Disruptions in myelin sheaths may influence both structural and functional aspects of circuits.
source: Moreover, many neurodegenerative diseases and affective disorders are associated with profound alterations in myelin (Gouw et al., 2008; Ihara et al., 2010; Stedehouder and Kushner, 2017), and recent studies indicate that demyelination triggers a dramatic decrease in excitatory synapses (Araújo et al., 2017; Werneburg et al., 2020), suggesting that disruptions in these sheaths may also influence both structural and functional aspects of circuits.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the association between demyelination and synaptic changes.

claim: Remyelination in the motor cortex is similar to that in the somatosensory cortex.
source: Our studies focused exclusively on regeneration in the somatosensory cortex of young adult mice. It is not yet known if these changes mimic regeneration in other cortical regions, although a recent pre-print indicates that remyelination in the motor cortex is similar (Bacmeister et al., 2020) https://doi.org/10.1101/2020.01.28.923656), or if the spatial and temporal aspects of myelin replacement in the cortex vary with age.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from a recent pre-print with supporting citation.

claim: Even subtle changes in oligodendrogenesis can alter behavioral performance.
source: As recent studies suggest that even subtle changes in oligodendrogenesis can alter behavioral performance (McKenzie et al., 2014; Xiao et al., 2016), the impact of these changes may be profound.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: In vivo two photon fluorescence microscopy allows visualization of oligodendrogenesis and myelin sheath formation in mammalian circuits at high resolution.
source: In vivo two photon fluorescence microscopy allows visualization of oligodendrogenesis and myelin sheath formation in mammalian circuits at high resolution, providing the means to define both the dynamics and specificity of regeneration (Hughes et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the capabilities of the imaging method used in the study with supporting citation.

claim: Myelination patterns are distinct among different neuron classes in the cortex.
source: Myelination patterns are distinct among different neuron classes in the cortex (Micheva et al., 2016; Stedehouder et al., 2017; Tomassy et al., 2014), and can be discontinuous, in which myelin segments along individual axons are separated by long regions of bare axon (Tomassy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Myelination in the cortex can be discontinuous, in which myelin segments along individual axons are separated by long regions of bare axon.
source: Myelination patterns are distinct among different neuron classes in the cortex (Micheva et al., 2016; Stedehouder et al., 2017; Tomassy et al., 2014), and can be discontinuous, in which myelin segments along individual axons are separated by long regions of bare axon (Tomassy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citation.

claim: The cerebral cortex is a highly layered structure, in which genetically and morphologically distinct neurons form specialized subnetworks.
source: The cerebral cortex is a highly layered structure, in which genetically and morphologically distinct neurons form specialized subnetworks (Lodato and Arlotta, 2015), raising the possibility that they may adopt different myelination patterns to optimize circuit capabilities (Micheva et al., 2016; Stedehouder et al., 2017; Tomassy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citation.

claim: Different cortical layers may adopt different myelination patterns to optimize circuit capabilities.
source: The cerebral cortex is a highly layered structure, in which genetically and morphologically distinct neurons form specialized subnetworks (Lodato and Arlotta, 2015), raising the possibility that they may adopt different myelination patterns to optimize circuit capabilities (Micheva et al., 2016; Stedehouder et al., 2017; Tomassy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as a possibility based on the layered structure of cortex with supporting citations.

claim: Both oligodendrocyte density and myelin content increase with depth from the cortical surface.
source: Indeed, myelination patterns are highly non-uniform across the cortex (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) and both oligodendrocyte density and myelin content increase with depth from the cortical surface (Hughes et al., 2018; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citation and imaging data in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Oligodendrocytes preferentially myelinate specific neurons, such as parvalbumin interneurons in layers II/III.
source: The high stability of oligodendrocytes and their preferential myelination of specific neurons, such as parvalbumin interneurons in layers II/III (Micheva et al., 2016; Stedehouder et al., 2017), suggest that preserving the overall pattern of myelin is important to optimize and sustain the processing capabilities of these circuits.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Preserving the overall pattern of myelin is important to optimize and sustain the processing capabilities of cortical circuits.
source: The high stability of oligodendrocytes and their preferential myelination of specific neurons, such as parvalbumin interneurons in layers II/III (Micheva et al., 2016; Stedehouder et al., 2017), suggest that preserving the overall pattern of myelin is important to optimize and sustain the processing capabilities of these circuits.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the stability and specificity of myelination patterns.

claim: Many neurodegenerative diseases and affective disorders are associated with profound alterations in myelin.
source: Moreover, many neurodegenerative diseases and affective disorders are associated with profound alterations in myelin (Gouw et al., 2008; Ihara et al., 2010; Stedehouder and Kushner, 2017), and recent studies indicate that demyelination triggers a dramatic decrease in excitatory synapses (Araújo et al., 2017; Werneburg et al., 2020), suggesting that disruptions in these sheaths may also influence both structural and functional aspects of circuits.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Reactive astrocytes can impair OPC differentiation by secreting cytokines.
source: Reactive astrocytes, a known pathological feature of both the cuprizone model and cortical demyelinating lesions (Chang et al., 2012; Skripuletz et al., 2008), can impair OPC differentiation by secreting cytokines (Kirby et al., 2019; Su et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2010), but whether reactive astrocytes impair recovery differently as a function of cortical depth is unknown.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Reactive astrocytes are a known pathological feature of both the cuprizone model and cortical demyelinating lesions.
source: Reactive astrocytes, a known pathological feature of both the cuprizone model and cortical demyelinating lesions (Chang et al., 2012; Skripuletz et al., 2008), can impair OPC differentiation by secreting cytokines (Kirby et al., 2019; Su et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2010), but whether reactive astrocytes impair recovery differently as a function of cortical depth is unknown.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Myelin debris can suppress oligodendrogenesis.
source: Inhibitory factors generated as a consequence of oligodendrocyte degeneration, such as myelin debris (Kotter et al., 2006), axonally expressed factors (LINGO1) (Mi et al., 2005), extracellular matrix components (chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans) (Lau et al., 2012), and reactive astrocytes (Back et al., 2005) may create a local zone of exclusion at sites of cell death reducing the probability of OPC differentiation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citation.

claim: LINGO1 is an axonally expressed factor that can suppress oligodendrogenesis.
source: Inhibitory factors generated as a consequence of oligodendrocyte degeneration, such as myelin debris (Kotter et al., 2006), axonally expressed factors (LINGO1) (Mi et al., 2005), extracellular matrix components (chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans) (Lau et al., 2012), and reactive astrocytes (Back et al., 2005) may create a local zone of exclusion at sites of cell death reducing the probability of OPC differentiation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citation.

claim: Chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans can suppress oligodendrogenesis.
source: Inhibitory factors generated as a consequence of oligodendrocyte degeneration, such as myelin debris (Kotter et al., 2006), axonally expressed factors (LINGO1) (Mi et al., 2005), extracellular matrix components (chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans) (Lau et al., 2012), and reactive astrocytes (Back et al., 2005) may create a local zone of exclusion at sites of cell death reducing the probability of OPC differentiation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citation.

evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the displacement of regenerated oligodendrocytes from original positions.

claim: Pro-myelination cues present in deeper cortical regions during development may no longer be present in the adult cortex.
source: It is also possible that positive, pro-myelination cues present in deeper cortical regions during development, similar to those described in the developing cerebellum (Goebbels et al., 2017), are no longer present in the adult cortex, rendering OPCs unable to sustain adequate remyelination.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for impaired regeneration in deeper layers with supporting citation.

claim: Oligodendrocytes have the capacity to form long processes.
source: The new locations of oligodendrocytes after a demyelinating event may not preclude these cells from myelinating the same axonal segments, as cortical oligodendrocytes can extend long cytoplasmic processes to form sheaths distant from the cell body (Chong et al., 2012; Murtie et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Cortical oligodendrocytes can extend long cytoplasmic processes to form sheaths distant from the cell body.
source: The new locations of oligodendrocytes after a demyelinating event may not preclude these cells from myelinating the same axonal segments, as cortical oligodendrocytes can extend long cytoplasmic processes to form sheaths distant from the cell body (Chong et al., 2012; Murtie et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Newly formed oligodendrocytes exhibited an initial period of refinement characterized by sheath extensions and retractions.
source: In both control and cuprizone-treated mice, newly generated oligodendrocytes exhibited an initial period of refinement after first appearance (governed by the onset of Mobp promoter activity and EGFP accumulation in the cytoplasm), characterized by sheath extensions and retractions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D), pruning of entire myelin sheaths and removal of cytoplasmic processes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–H), before reaching a stable morphology (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I,J).
evidence: This is a finding from longitudinal reconstruction analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Newly formed oligodendrocytes undergo pruning of entire myelin sheaths and removal of cytoplasmic processes before reaching a stable morphology.
source: In both control and cuprizone-treated mice, newly generated oligodendrocytes exhibited an initial period of refinement after first appearance (governed by the onset of Mobp promoter activity and EGFP accumulation in the cytoplasm), characterized by sheath extensions and retractions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D), pruning of entire myelin sheaths and removal of cytoplasmic processes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–H), before reaching a stable morphology (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I,J).
evidence: This is a finding from longitudinal reconstruction analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The final position of the cytoplasmic process along the length of the sheaths was randomly distributed along the length of the internode.
source: The final position of the cytoplasmic process along the length of the sheaths (the likely point of sheath initiation) was randomly distributed along the length of the internode (Figure 3—figure supplement 1K,L).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of process-sheath contact points shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1K,L.

claim: Remyelination may be opportunistic and based on chance interactions between processes and local axon segments.
source: These results suggest that remyelination may be opportunistic and based, at least initially, on chance interactions between processes and local axon segments.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that oligodendrocytes form both replaced and novel sheaths based on their territory.

claim: Premyelinating oligodendrocytes have a highly radial morphology.
source: This finding is consistent with the highly radial morphology of premyelinating oligodendrocytes (Trapp et al., 1997), which would be optimized for local search of the surrounding volume rather than directed, regional targeting of subsets of axons.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citation.

claim: The radial morphology of premyelinating oligodendrocytes is optimized for local search of the surrounding volume rather than directed, regional targeting of subsets of axons.

evidence: This is an inference about the functional significance of oligodendrocyte morphology with supporting citation.

claim: In control mice, almost all internodes (99.1 ± 0.5%) present at baseline remained after 5 weeks.
source: Consistent with previous findings (Hill et al., 2018; Hughes et al., 2018), in control mice almost all internodes (99.1 ± 0.5%) present at baseline remained after 5 weeks (Figure 5A, gray processes), demonstrating the high stability of myelin sheaths within the cortex.
evidence: This is a finding from myelin sheath tracing analysis shown in Figure 5A with supporting citations.

claim: Generation of new oligodendrocytes led to the appearance of a substantial proportion (25.8 ± 8.7%) of novel sheaths in control mice.
source: Generation of new oligodendrocytes within this area led to the appearance of a substantial proportion (25.8 ± 8.7%) of novel sheaths (Figure 5A, green processes).
evidence: This is a finding from myelin sheath tracing analysis in control mice shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The time course over which nodal components are removed from demyelinated axons could influence the subsequent distribution of myelin.
source: The time course over which these nodal components are removed from demyelinated axons could influence the subsequent distribution of myelin, with prolonged demyelinating injuries leading to greater loss of remyelination specificity.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the relationship between nodal component stability and remyelination specificity.

claim: Prolonged demyelinating injuries may lead to greater loss of remyelination specificity.

evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the consequences of prolonged demyelination.

claim: Changes to axonal diameter might alter the distribution of replaced myelin sheaths.

evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about potential factors affecting remyelination patterns.

claim: Experience-dependent changes in myelin appear to occur primarily through addition of new sheaths arising from oligodendrogenesis.
source: Experience-dependent changes in myelin appear to occur primarily through addition of new sheaths arising from oligodendrogenesis (Hughes et al., 2018), although changes in myelin sheath thickness may also occur (Dutta et al., 2018; Gibson et al., 2014).

claim: Changes in myelin sheath thickness may occur in response to experience.

claim: Oligodendrocytes perform crucial roles in the CNS, including enhancing the propagation of action potentials and reducing the metabolic cost to do so.
source: Oligodendrocytes perform crucial roles in the CNS, enhancing the propagation of action potentials and reducing the metabolic cost to do so, providing metabolic support for axons far removed from their cell bodies and controlling excitability by influencing the distribution of voltage-gated channels and promoting clearance of extracellular potassium.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about oligodendrocyte functions.

claim: Myelination patterns are established progressively over many months in the cerebral cortex.
source: The organization of myelin in the cerebral cortex is remarkably diverse, with densities of myelin sheaths varying between cortical regions, between axons from different classes of neurons and even along individual axons within a given area. These patterns are established progressively over many months, creating an extended developmental time course that results in pronounced increases in myelin through adolescence and adulthood.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cortical myelination development.

claim: Oligodendrogenesis and myelination can be enhanced by life experience and may be critical to certain forms of learning.
source: Although progressive, oligodendrogenesis and myelination can be enhanced by life experience and may be critical to certain forms of learning (Gibson et al., 2014; Hughes et al., 2018; McKenzie et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Oligodendrocytes and their complement of myelin sheaths are resistant to environmental changes such as sensory enrichment.
source: However, once formed, oligodendrocytes and their complement of myelin sheaths are extraordinarily stable, with cell survival and sheath position varying little over months and are resistant to environmental changes such as sensory enrichment, in accordance with the high stability of myelin proteins and the persistence of oligodendrocytes in the human CNS (Yeung et al., 2014).
